title: Thrombocytopenia in an EGFR 19 Exon-Deficient Bilateral Diffuse LUAD with ARDS Treated with ECMO and Osimertinib: A Case Report
author: Donghai Liang; Fei Zhou; Chen Xu; Lili Zou; Tao Jiang; Haijun Lu; Chunliu Meng
text:
Abstract
Introduction
EGFR-sensitive mutations bilateral diffuse lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) complicated with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is relatively rare. It is important to consider whether EGFR-TKI can be simultaneously received when treating with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and anti-infective therapy in these patients, and what adverse events should be noted?
Case Presentation
We report a case of EGFR 19 exon-deficient bilateral diffuse LUAD complicated with ARDS. When treated with ECMO and anti-infective therapy, the patient received oral osimertinib anti-tumor therapy simultaneously. The tumor receded, but eventually irreversible thrombocytopenia developed.
Conclusion
For patients with severe lung cancer, anti-tumor efficacy and adverse events should be closely observed during anti-tumor therapy.
Keywords: Bilateral diffuse lung adenocarcinoma, Acute respiratory distress syndrome, Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, Osimertinib, Thrombocytopenia
Introduction
Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is a common pathological type of lung cancer [1], most of which show isolated peripheral lesions. Bilateral diffuse LUAD is rare, especially in newly diagnosed patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). About half of nonsmoking Asian women with LUAD have epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-sensitive mutations [2, 3]. Clinically, about 10–30% of newly diagnosed LUAD patients are elderly or frail, such as performance status score of 2–4, with severe cardiovascular disease, etc. [4]. For elderly and frail LUAD patients with EGFR-sensitive mutations, first- or third-generation EGFR-TKIs can be accepted in the first line [5, 6]. However, for EGFR-sensitive mutations bilateral diffuse LUAD patients complicated with ARDS, whether TKI can be simultaneously received when receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and anti-infective therapy has not been reported. While treatments are used simultaneously, what adverse events (AEs) should be noted? In this case, we reported an AE with irreversible thrombocytopenia in the above patient.
Case Report
A 48-year-old female patient with no smoking history and disease history developed cough, chest tightness, dyspnea during March 2024, with symptoms gradually worsened. On March 23, 2024, the patient developed fever with temperature up to 38.5°C. Blood routine test (RT) showed leukocytes 6.05 × 109/L, neutrophils 4.34 × 109/L, platelets 331 × 109/L. Chest CT on March 24, 2024, showed multiple nodular and flaky high-density shadows of varying sizes were diffused in bilateral pulmonary. Tumor markers showed SCC 18.5 ng/mL, NSE 33.50 ng/mL, pro-GRP 78.1 pg/mL, CA-199 17.20 ng/mL. Influenza-A virus test was positive. Bronchoscopy showed significant congestion and edema in the wall mucosa of the left and right bronchial tubes. Biopsy pathology showed adenocarcinoma. The patient’s dyspnea worsened rapidly. Arterial blood-gas analysis on March 24, 2024, showed PaO2 47 mm Hg, SpO2 83.2%. Mechanical ventilation was used urgently, but PaO2 and SpO2 did not improve significantly. On March 25, 2024, the patient was transferred to ICU. Clinical diagnosis was LUAD, severe pneumonia, ARDS, respiratory failure.
When transferred to ICU, her SpO2 was consistently below 85%. So, ECMO was administered. Meanwhile, sputum culture and fungal, aspergillus, influenza virus, novel coronavirus, tuberculosis, mycoplasma pulmonary tests were negative. Based on clinical experience, symptomatic treatment was also given, such as piperacillin tazobactam combined with minocycline antibacterial, posaconazole antifungal, oseltamivir antiviral, glucocorticoid to inhibit inflammation, low dose of norepinephrine to maintain blood pressure, anticoagulation. Chest CT on March 28, 2024, showed bilateral pneumonia, possible tumor not excluded; right pleural effusion; several slightly larger lymph nodes in the upper and lower clavicular region and mediastinum (Fig. 1). Pathological consultation on March 31, 2024, showed non-small cell lung cancer, predisposed to adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical results showed TTF-1 (+), napsin A (+). Blood genetic test (next-generation sequencing) was proceeded to guide follow-up treatment.
On the night of April 1, 2024, the patient developed airway bleeding. Blood coagulation routine test (CRT) on April 2, 2024, showed prothrombin time (PT) 13.00 s, international normalized ratio (INR) 1.12INR, activated partial thrombin time (APTT) 33.60 s, thrombin time (TT) 17.00 s, fibrinogen 5.28 g/L, antithrombin-III 106.00%, D-dimer 1,740.00 ng/mL. Blood RT showed leukocytes 15.34 × 109/L, hemoglobin 86.00 g/L, platelets 171 × 109/L. Emergency bronchoscopy showed that there were neoplasms on the left and right main bronchus, with no exception of blood clots. Airway hemostasis was administered and anticoagulant therapy was discontinued. Intermittent reexamination of blood RT and CRT showed no significant change in platelets, but D-dimer increased significantly (Fig. 2; online suppl. Fig. S1; for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000544788).
On April 9, 2024, arterial blood-gas analysis showed PaO2 105 mm Hg, SpO2 98.5%. The tracheal tube was removed, and SpO2 was satisfactory. On April 10, 2024, blood culture indicated positive for Gram-positive coccus (Staphylococcus epidermidis). Basing on drug susceptibility test result, vancomycin was added. Blood genetic test showed EGFR 19-exon deletion mutation 4.82%; osimertinib 80 mg QD was started. Blood RT+CRP on April 12, 2024, showed leukocytes 5.94 × 109/L, hemoglobin 69 g/L, platelets 148 × 109/L, CRP 19.02 mg/L. Blood CRT showed PT 13.90 s, INR 1.20 INR, APTT 41.10 s, TT 21.90 s, fibrinogen 1.66 g/L, antithrombin-III 89.00%, D-dimer 21,020.00 ng/mL. Since D-dimer was significantly elevated, anticoagulant therapy was continued.
Sputum culture on April 15, 2024, showed carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (+), so ceftazidime-avibactam combined with vancomycin was adjusted to antibacterial and posaconazole, prevention of fungal infection. Meanwhile, the patient had pain in left waist and groin area. CT scan showed large flake and nodular solid shadow in bilateral lung, which slightly decreased in scope compared with the front part; mixed density shadow in left retroperitoneal iliopsoas area, considering hematoma; pelvic effusion (blood) (Figs. 1, 3). Blood RT+CRP showed leukocytes 2.99 × 109/L, hemoglobin 68g/L, platelets 90 × 109/L, CRP 16.94 mg/L. Anticoagulants should be stopped immediately. Vascular intervention recommended conservative treatment. Hemostasis and red blood cell transfusion were given. Night blood RT on April 15, 2024, showed leukocyte 9.11 × 109/L, hemoglobin 51 g/L, platelets 73 × 109/L.
Due to continuous decrease of hemoglobin and platelets, side effects of osimertinib should not be excluded, a half dose was reduced, and component blood was transfused again. Blood RT on April 16, 2024, showed leukocytes 10.34 × 109/L, hemoglobin 65 g/L, platelets 115 × 109/L.
On April 17, 2024, the patient had shortness of breath, 40 times/min, and finger pulse dropped to 80%. So, mechanical ventilation was given again immediately. Review blood RT+CRP showed leukocytes 12.61 × 109/L, hemoglobin 55 g/L, platelets 90 × 109/L. Active bleeding is considered as hemoglobin has declined again. Reexamination CT showed the left retroperitoneal space-iliopsoas area had a mixed density, which was significantly larger than the anterior area, pelvic effusion (blood), more than before (Fig. 3). Lumbar arteriography and embolization were performed immediately, and red blood cell, platelets were transfused multiple times. Intermittent reexamination of blood RT showed hemoglobin was maintained at 70–80 g/L, but platelets continued to decline, with the lowest drop to 24 × 109/L (Fig. 2). Platelets continued to be transfused several times, but they continued to decline repeatedly and could not be improved (Fig. 2). On April 24, 2024, reexamination CT showed bilateral pulmonary hilum patchy nodular solid shadow, slightly reduced than before; there was a mixed density in the left retroperitoneal iliopsoas area with little change compared with the anterior area (Fig. 1, 3).
Discussion
In this case, the patient had a bilateral diffuse LUAD with EGFR 19-exon deletion mutation complicated with ARDS, who received ECMO, anti-infective therapy, and osimertinib simultaneously. Reexamination on days 5 and 14 after oral osimertinib indicated tumor reduction. However, it is worth noting that the patient developed thrombocytopenia after 5 days of osimertinib and continued to decline rapidly. The causes of thrombocytopenia may be as follows: osimertinib AE, drug pharmacokinetic interaction, and severe infection.
Thrombocytopenia is one of the AEs for osimertinib. In AURA and AURA2 studies, 54% patients experienced thrombocytopenia and 1.6% patients experienced grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia [7, 8]. There are two types of drug-induced thrombocytopenia: drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia (DITP) and non-DITP. The typical manifestation of DITP is a rapid decrease in platelets at 5–14 days after drug treatment, which can be <20 × 109/L, often accompanied by bleeding. The platelets do not begin to recover until 5–7 half-lives have elapsed [9–12]. The typical manifestation of non-DITP is a slow decrease in platelets, generally not <20 × 109/L, and a rapid recovery of platelets after withdrawal [12]. During the administration of osimertinib, if the patient has a rapid reduction of platelets below 50 × 109/L, osimertinib should be suspended after excluding other causes. After platelets rose to >100 × 109/L, osimertinib can be resumed. If platelets decline is slow, and not <50 × 109/L, the patient can continue to take osimertinib, while taking medical intervention. In this case, the patient experienced rapid platelet reduction of as little as 24 × 109/L after 5 days of oral osimertinib [13]. After osimertinib reduction and discontinuation, platelets transfusion was administered; platelets continue to decline rapidly and cannot be maintained; DITP is more likely.
In vitro studies have confirmed that osimertinib is mainly metabolized by CYP3A4/5. When used in combination with CYP3A4 inhibitors, plasma concentrations of osimertinib active substances can increase [14–17]. In pharmacokinetic studies of osimertinib, combined with itraconazole, a CYP3A4 inhibitor, it resulted in about 20% increase in AUC of drug concentration and Cmax [16, 17]. Osimertinib also increased the exposure of P-glycoprotein (P-gp) substrate. In this case, posaconazole was administered throughout treatment. Posaconazole is an inhibitor of CYP3A4, metabolized primarily by UDP glucuronidase, and is a substrate for the efflux of P-gp. In drug label, 7–11% patients receiving posaconazole 300 mg/day experienced thrombocytopenia [18, 19]. The pharmacokinetic interference of osimertinib and posaconazole, combined with slightly lower creatinine clearance, may increase each other’s blood drug concentration, resulting in rapid platelet decline.
Severe infection may be another cause. It has been reported that the main causes of infection-induced thrombocytopenia are decreased platelet production, increased platelet destruction and consumption, and platelet apoptosis [20]. The main manifestations were myelosuppression caused by severe infection, inhibition of bone marrow megakaryocytes by bacterial endotoxin, and hematopoietic negative regulatory factors, resulting in reduced platelet production; bacteria and metabolites activate complement through immune pathways, bacterial endotoxin damage to vascular endothelium, anti-platelet antibodies, disseminated intravascular coagulation due to severe infection, hemodialysis or blood purification, resulting in increased platelet destruction. In this case, the patient had bacteremia, which caused disseminated intravascular coagulation that may be one cause of thrombocytopenia.
Conclusion
This case reports an EGFR-sensitive mutant bilateral diffuse LUAD patient complicated with ARDS, who received ECMO, anti-infective therapy, and osimertinib simultaneously. It is worth emphasizing that, for such lung cancer patients with severe infection, while paying attention to anti-tumor efficacy, we should also pay attention to platelet changes to prevent the occurrence of severe thrombocytopenia.
